The ThoxMini slot ships its Wave C build (gate 47/49, tying the fleet's best gate score; probe 3/6) as its documented baseline — merged, converted, endpoint-served and Ollama-published, with the probe caveat stated on its card — because its two fix-cycle adapters were held (C.1: gate 46/49, probe 3/6; C.2: gate 44/49 with perfect verified and known_false splits, probe 5/6, held on the probe's tool-routing check). The ThoxClip slot ships the prior published ThoxClip-Qwen3-0.6B as its documented baseline: all three of its program adapters (Wave C 43/49, C.1 37/49, C.2 39/49) are held in their repositories with their failures on their cards. All three flagship Ollama names are verified registry-side by layer digest (§9.4). The final program tally is §9.5. No adapter in this program has been qualified on physical device hardware; hardware qualification is a separate claim with no evidence in this program.

1Introduction

A device fleet that answers questions about itself has a factuality problem before it has a capability problem. A 0.5B-parameter assistant on a keychain device will not out-reason a frontier model, and it does not need to. It needs to state the company's published facts correctly, decline the facts the company has not published, refuse to repeat claims the company has already established are false, and stop. Every one of those behaviours is trainable, and every one is measurable. The THOX edge-model program has therefore been organized, since its first wave, around a single question: does this artifact, measured weights-only against a fixed question set derived from the canonical facts card, tell the truth more reliably than the artifact it would replace?

Wave C is the fourth step in that program and the first run as a slate rather than as a sequence of individual fixes. The prior steps, stated briefly because this paper's baselines come from them: Wave A established the gate itself and the first baselines, including a 19/49 score for the 0.8B tier that remains the only valid measurement of that tier. Wave B expanded the training corpus from 205 rows to 982, retrained the edge line on it, and produced the fleet's strongest result — ThoxEdge-0.5B at 47/49 — alongside two lessons that shape everything in this paper. The first lesson is that a gate score is only as trustworthy as its serving path: the Wave B 0.8B run's 0/49 was produced by a serving layer returning answers in a channel the scorer could not see, and the fleet held the line unpublished for weeks rather than act on a number it could not trust. The second lesson is that corpus hygiene is a safety property: ten corpus rows that repeated fabricated claims inside denials had to be rewritten before retraining, because the gate fails any answer that repeats a known-false claim, even one it is denying.

Wave C's order, from the CTO on October 28, 2026, was direct: use Hugging Face resources to train, fine-tune, or finish the device models; produce a flagship model for each device; provision whatever training capacity the work needs. The program that executed that order had four moving parts, and this paper takes them in order. First, a survey defended each device tier's base model against the latest flagship-class releases in its size class, screened under the company's license policy, because a fine-tune inherits its base's license, architecture, and failure modes. Second, all four flagships trained on the same 982-row Wave B corpus through the THOX compute plane, a registry-and-launcher system that dispatches one Hugging Face Job per fine-tune under the Thox-ai namespace. Third, each adapter faced the same publishing authority: the 49-question factuality gate, run as a follow-up job in the same infrastructure, plus an additional six-prompt probe for the one flagship whose deployment contract includes a grounding system prompt. Fourth, promotion followed a written rule — publish only on improvement, never with a known-false hard failure outstanding — applied by a named decision-maker whose rulings, including the two negative rulings in this wave, are recorded in the model cards themselves.

The results are mixed, and this paper reports them in that form. The Mini flagship's gate score ties the fleet record; its probe exposes three specific behaviours that keep it from shipping. The Air flagship fills an empty slot with a credible baseline and one fabrication that keeps it from shipping. The Edge retrain clears its bar outright and is promoted. The Clip retrain proves the corpus diagnosis on the count and is held anyway, on the two failures its gate exists to catch. A program paper that printed only the first of those sentences would be marketing. The discipline this program runs on — the gate, the publish rule, the named failures, the held promotions — is the actual product, and the paper's job is to show it working, including where it says no. It also shows the discipline iterating: two fix cycles (§9) revised the corpus twice, changed two training recipes on evidence, produced one further promotion and five further held adapters, and closed under a stopping rule that ships each slot's best measured artifact rather than its newest.

Contributions. (1) A defended flagship slate for a five-device ecosystem, with the survey method and license policy stated precisely enough to repeat next cycle. (2) A training system description, including a worked cost model, that another engineer can operate from. (3) A dependency failure taxonomy from a real multi-model training wave: three distinct first-attempt failures and one interpreter-version failure, each traced to root cause, with the profile system that resulted. (4) An evaluation design and its full results for all four flagships, including the negative cases and the losing recipe comparison, stated against per-model publish bars fixed before the runs. (5) Two executed fix cycles (Wave C.1, Wave C.2) in which every item traces to a named observed failure, closing with the final program tally against the program's completion bar: trained, published, carded, and documented. (6) A post-publication served-path evaluation (added in v0.4.2): every shipped tag gated and probed exactly as served from the registry, before and after a serving-configuration fix, with the untuned bases gated bare and grounded as the attribution baseline the first editions lacked (§8.6).

2Definitions and terminology

The program's vocabulary is operational: each term below names a decision or a measurement, not a marketing category.

Flagship. The one assistant model designated, per device, as that device's primary fine-tune: the model whose card carries the device's name, whose gate result is the device's published factuality claim, and whose promotion state decides what ships. A device has exactly one flagship slot. Before Wave C, the ThoxAir slot was empty — the device shipped a 16M-parameter role model and otherwise rode another tier's weights plus mesh escalation — and the ThoxKey slot is filled by design by the ThoxMini flagship, because ThoxKey runs no assistant model on-device and is served by a host (ThoxBeam) running the Mini flagship payload.

Adapter. The trainable artifact this program produces: a LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) [12] update, rank 32, stored with its tokenizer in a model repository. The compute plane's runs — the Wave C and Wave C.1 cycles — train that update against a frozen, 4-bit-quantized base (QLoRA [13]); the program's full-precision LoRA artifacts (the Wave B reference build and the promoted Wave C.2 Air build) are defined in §8.5 and §9.3, where the recipe comparison is measured. An adapter is not a servable model. It becomes one only at promotion, when it is merged into the base weights and converted for the serving stack. Every quality claim in this paper is a claim about base + adapter measured together, never about the adapter alone.

Gate (GATE49). The fleet's 49-question factuality gate: a fixed question set in four categories — verified (12), unknown (26), known_false (10), pricing (1) — derived from the canonical THOX facts card, each answer trait-scored on a 0–5 scale, reported as questions passed of 49 plus the mean trait score. Section 7 specifies it fully.

Hard failure. An answer the scorer charges with asserting a claim the facts card marks false or not public: it repeats a known-false claim (including inside a denial), asserts an unpublished figure or specification, or names a fabricated entity, place, or amount. Hard failures are counted separately from low trait scores. Two classes must be distinguished, because the program's rulings turned on the distinction (§7.5): a false-assertion hard failure states a false or unpublished fact; a detector-form hard failure states no false fact but is not recognized by the gate's decline detector as a decline (for example, a premise correction stated in card-true terms, or a trained short-decline form the detector's vocabulary misses). Earlier editions of this paper stated a blanket zero-hard-failure policy — any hard failure blocks promotion regardless of the headline score. The rulings as actually made applied the narrower rule written in §7.5: false-assertion hard failures block; detector-form hard failures are recorded on the card and do not, by themselves, block. Section 7.5 prints the full decision function and every deviation from the blanket statement, so the record no longer depends on which paragraph a reader believes.

Promotion. The act of making an adapter the device flagship: merging it, converting it, replacing the published weights, and filling the model card's evaluation section from the gate report. Promotion is a decision, recorded with a named decider and date, and reversible by the CTO. Its opposite in this paper is a held adapter: trained, published as a candidate artifact, gated, documented — and not shipped.

Documented baseline. The shipping tier for a slot whose best measured artifact did not earn promotion: the artifact is merged, converted, published, and carded like a promotion, its card's first section states the caveat that kept it from promotion, and no flagship claim is made for it. A documented baseline ships under its own written conditions — gate measured, failures named on the card, and, where the record requires it (ThoxClip), a serving contract such as grounding-required. It is not a flagship and is never described as one; §9.5 records which slots closed in this tier.

Null policy (reference responder). A constant responder that answers every gate question with the facts card's prescribed decline form and nothing else ("I do not have verified information about that. Please check thox.ai for the verified information."). Scored through the program's own scorer it achieves 25/49 with zero hard failures (§7.1). It is the floor every publish bar and every result in this paper is restated against in §7.3: a gate that a constant string passes at 25/49 measures abstention discipline first and knowledge second, and this paper's numbers are reported with that stated.

The four reported metrics. Alongside the headline pass count, results are decomposed as: verified recall (verified questions passed of 12); abstention rate (unknown questions passed of 26 — declines in a form the detector recognizes, asserting nothing unpublished); unauthorized-disclosure rate (unknown-category hard failures of 26 — answers that assert unpublished information); and false-assertion rate (known_false hard failures of 10 — answers that repeat or endorse a claim the card establishes is false). GATE49 is, precisely, a disclosure-conformance and verified-recall instrument; it is not a general factuality benchmark, and §10 carries the consequence.

Dependency profile. A named, pinned set of package versions plus the container image and bootstrap procedure a training or gate job runs under. The compute plane's profiles — pinned, latest, and the fleet profile created during this wave — are specified in Section 6. In this program a profile is part of the recipe: changing it changes the training signal (one profile's TRL version supervises the full prompt where another masks it), so results are always reported with the profile that produced them.

Baseline. A model's own prior gate result, measured weights-only under the gate's conventions, against which improvement is judged. Where a slot has no prior result, the first gated run establishes the baseline and cannot, by itself, constitute improvement over anything; promotion from an established baseline requires the additional conditions in Section 7.3.

Facts card. The canonical, versioned statement of THOX's published facts (facts card v1.1.0 in this wave) from which both the training corpus's factual rows and the gate's questions derive. Corpus and gate share one source deliberately: the gate measures whether the model learned the card, and the card is the company's public record, not a benchmark author's invention.

3The flagship slate and its defense

3.1 Survey method

A fine-tune cannot outrun its base. It inherits the base's license — a derivative cannot be freer than its base — its architecture's support in the training and serving stack, and a measurable share of its failure modes. Wave C therefore began with a survey, executed on October 28, 2026 against live Hugging Face API reads, whose full record is the program's survey document. The method, stated so it can be repeated:

  1. Screen. Start from the CTO's screen — license Apache-2.0, edge tag, sorted by downloads — applied through the Hub API. The screen produced the candidate field across all tiers; the survey document records the candidate set it produced, tier by tier.
  2. Widen. Add the MIT/BSD families and every named family in each size class (Qwen, Phi, SmolLM, Granite, Ministral, OLMo, Gemma, Llama, LFM), so the screen's filter cannot silently exclude a legitimate challenger.
  3. Verify licenses at the weights. For every finalist, the license was read from the repository's card metadata and license tags — the license that covers the weights, not the repository's code license and not a search filter's guess. This step is where the LFM line failed: its cards declare a license name of "lfm1.0" with an other tag, whatever the marketing surface suggests.
  4. Verify shape. Parameter totals from safetensors metadata, architecture from the config's model type, creation dates and download counts from the API — recorded per candidate in the survey's tier tables.
  5. Weigh fleet evidence over vendor claims. Vendor-reported capability is labeled as such wherever this paper repeats it. Where the fleet has its own measurement of a base — a prior gate score, an evaluation on fleet hardware — that measurement outranks any published benchmark in the verdict reasoning, because the flagship decision is a decision about this fleet's stack, prompts, and gate.

License policy applied. Apache-2.0 first; then MIT, BSD-3-Clause, BSD-2-Clause, CC0-1.0, ISC — all permitting commercial use, fine-tuning, and proprietary modification. Llama community licenses and Gemma terms are conditional: flagged wherever they appear, never a first choice. The LFM Open License is not on the approved list — its commercial-use ceiling (flagged in the company's IP register at under $10M revenue) disqualifies it for commercial device products — and the Falcon LLM License fails on the same other-tag ground. One further rule from the company's model policy: a fine-tune of a permissive base is a Track A asset (THOX's improvements are its own contribution, offered under the base's license terms; the base remains under its license, with attribution obligations preserved — §15 records how those obligations are currently discharged), and no derivative is ever described as freer than its base.

ThoxMini — Phi-4-mini, KEEP. The incumbent had won the fleet's own head-to-head: in the fleet Mac workstation evaluation and the October 28 thinking-off retest, the strongest challenger in class (Qwen3-4B) won tool-routing outright but failed an arithmetic check (17 + 25 answered as 32) and failed the grounding trap by inventing a "ThoxMini custom AI chip"; Phi-4-mini completed and was selected to ship, under the standing rule that whichever model ships carries the grounded device-facts system prompt, never bare. Against the new field — Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (Apache-2.0, 4.02B), Ministral-3-3B-Instruct-2512 (Apache-2.0, newest in class, vendor-reported edge-class leading), granite-4.2-3b (Apache-2.0, newest release in class), SmolLM3-3B (Apache-2.0) — no challenger was clearly better on two axes without a regression: Ministral's conditional-generation (vision) architecture is a stack regression against the proven phi3 fine-tune/GGUF path and its edge is vendor-reported only; Qwen3-4B's refresh carries the family's fresh negative fleet evidence and no local eval. The named next-cycle challengers, in order, are granite-4.2-3b, Ministral-3-3B-Instruct-2512, and SmolLM3-3B.

ThoxAir — Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, KEEP, into an empty slot. Air had no flagship: a 16M role model is not an assistant baseline. The decisive fact about this base is fleet evidence, not novelty — this exact base, under this recipe, on this corpus, already produced ThoxEdge-0.5B's 47/49 in Wave B. The Air flagship is therefore the same base with an Air-specific adapter and its own repository and gate run; it does not inherit the Edge model's score, and Section 8.1 shows why that separation matters: on its own run it scored lower. The strongest challenger, SmolLM2-360M-Instruct, is a better size fit and vendor-reported comparable-or-better per parameter, but recency is a wash, the license ties, and it has no fleet proof. The tier's most recent release, LFM2.5-350M, was disqualified on license before capability was considered.

ThoxClip — Qwen3-0.6B, KEEP. The published Clip model's 22/49 was diagnosed in Wave B as a corpus problem, not a base problem: it was finished on the 205-row predecessor corpus while its siblings retrained on 982 rows. Wave C tests exactly that diagnosis — same base, full corpus. The one newer same-family option, Qwen3.5-0.8B, changes the architecture class to conditional-generation and inherits a serving artifact the fleet has documented for that family (Section 7.1); switching bases to chase it would confound the corpus test. LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct was disqualified on license.

ThoxEdge-0.8B — Qwen3.5-0.8B, KEEP. The latest generation in its class; nothing newer, cleaner-licensed, or same-sized exists to switch to. Its held Wave B publish is a serving-layer artifact, not a base defect (Section 7.1), and the chosen fix — retrain through the plane, gate through Transformers — is this wave's Edge entry.

ThoxKey role tier — SmolLM2, SWITCH. The one clean switch in the survey. SmolLM2-135M/360M-Instruct are the direct generational successors to the incumbent SmolLM v1 bases at identical sizes and the identical LlamaForCausalLM architecture — zero stack change — at the same Apache-2.0 license, shipping instruct variants the v1 line lacks, vendor-reported as a large capability jump over v1. The training-token figures are corrected in this edition from the vendor cards: SmolLM2-135M was trained on 2 trillion tokens and SmolLM2-360M on 4 trillion (the 11-trillion figure belongs to SmolLM2-1.7B, not to these sizes), against 600 billion tokens for SmolLM v1 at the same two sizes — vendor figures, labeled as such. Better on generation and capability, tied on license, fit, and size. The switch applies to the next role-tier training wave; the published ThoxNano models are not retroactively changed, and ThoxKey's flagship proper remains the host-served Phi-4-mini fine-tune above.

Two exclusions deserve explicit statement because they will recur every cycle. First, the entire LFM line — LFM2, LFM2.5, and LFM3 at every size — is disqualified for new picks in every tier under the license policy, including two candidates (LFM2.5-350M for Air, LFM2.5-1.2B for Clip) that were otherwise the most recent releases in their classes. License is a gate, not a tiebreaker. Second, no candidate was adopted on vendor-reported capability alone; every KEEP verdict rests at least partly on fleet measurement, and every challenger displaced only where the advantage was structural (generation, architecture fit, license) rather than a benchmark claim.

4The training corpus

All four flagships trained on one corpus, so that cross-model gate differences are attributable to the model and the recipe rather than to the data: train_wave_b.jsonl, 982 rows, in the private dataset repository Thox-ai/thox-factory-sft-v5. Each row is a dictionary with a messages list of exactly [system, user, assistant] turns and a meta key the trainer's renderer ignores. The corpus was built in Wave B: 838 newly authored rows plus 144 rows retained verbatim from the predecessor corpus, after 49 predecessor rows were superseded by canonical rewrites of the same prompts during deduplication.

Composition. Table 2 gives the domain split recorded at construction. Factual grounding dominates by design: company facts, device support, tool routing, and campaign rows together are 78% of the corpus, because the gate the models must pass is a factuality gate.

Sources. Factual rows derive from the THOX facts card (v1.1.0 line) and the live thox.ai campaign oracle. Recorded design decisions that matter for interpreting gate results: campaign figures (kit prices $189/$419/$699 with limits 150/100/50; Early Bird singles $79/$119/$239/$319 — the post-November-2 prices, with Super Early Bird singles holding through November 2, 2026, 11:59 PM CT; delivery estimate February–April 2027) are taught only in campaign-framed questions, while generic price questions train a decline plus a pointer to thox.ai — the behaviour the gate's pricing category expects. One correction, recorded in §9.2 and stated here so this section does not assert what the fix cycles disproved: the Wave B corpus also contained eighteen generic-price rows teaching a different answer shape (a statement that the amount is not stated, plus a description of where pricing appears), and a model reproduced one of those rows verbatim at gate time and was scored as not declining. The corpus and the gate disagreed about the pricing form; C.1 rewrote all eighteen rows into the canonical decline. No processor or chipset specifics appear anywhere in the corpus; dedicated processor-decline rows were added instead.

Hygiene, and why it is part of the method. Twelve predecessor rows asserting device chipset identities that contradict the facts card were excluded at construction of the 982-row corpus. Those twelve rows were part of the 205-row predecessor file itself — and the published ThoxClip-Qwen3-0.6B weights that still ship in the Clip slot (§8.4, §9.5) were finished on that 205-row file, so the shipped Clip weights did train on the twelve rows later excluded. That is stated here, in the corpus section, because it is a fact about the shipped artifact's provenance, not a footnote to it. Then, after construction, a pre-retrain scan found the subtler failure: ten authored rows whose assistant answers repeated fabricated names and figures inside denials of them — answers of the form "no, THOX has not raised $X from firm Y," which teach the model to emit X and Y in exactly the contexts where the gate probes for them. Those ten rows were rewritten to deny without naming the fabrication, the rescan came back clean for every fabricated string (founder names, firms, amounts, cities) in any assistant turn, and the one retrain already running on the unpatched file was killed about fifteen minutes in and relaunched so that all retrains share one identical dataset. Section 8 shows this failure class — fabrication leaking through a decline — recurring at evaluation time in both completed flagships. The scope of that scan must be stated exactly, because §9.2 found what it missed: it was a blocklist string scan, which finds only strings someone already knew to look for. It did not catch rows naming models that do not exist (found in C.1's construction audit, §9.2) or rows whose form contradicted the gate (the eighteen pricing rows above). Corpus hygiene in this program is therefore a partially measured property: content strings were scanned; entity validity and form conformance were established only when the fix cycles audited for them. A validator built on an allowed-entity list derived from the facts card, with every decline row passed through the gate's own detector before training, is the recorded remedy and has not yet been built.

Provenance. The corpus file as first published hashed to SHA-256 9ddf814ddd6a5f057eab4842461bce24c7d2bc082ac1d26576b7cb6fcbfe50e8. After the ten-row correction, the corrected corpus — the version every Wave B retrain and every Wave C run consumed — hashes to SHA-256 6665a8cbd79197c61a9db8119b743faedc3e469407364bb553ec9478e90a5784 (982 rows, count unchanged), republished at dataset-repository HEAD e76e1b027cde01d47c0dffaa9fbbc15c2ba43f93. The same repository also holds the predecessor file train.jsonl (205 rows, SHA-256 ac118a250bc989c9478ec7e4ebdcc706e12e489979b02e6bf1af8b831f8b2514); the flagship registry entries name train_wave_b.jsonl explicitly, because anyone "simplifying" the data path back to the shorter filename silently cuts the corpus by 79%. The corpus contains no user or customer data and no third-party text corpora. The only personal data it contains are the founders' own names, titles, and roles, drawn from the facts card and included at their direction — they are the program's principals, and the card is the company's public record of them. The 838 newly authored rows were authored in-house by the program team from the facts card and the campaign oracle, under the construction record cited above; no external text corpus and no third-party dataset was ingested. (Earlier editions stated flatly that the corpus contains "no personal data"; that was imprecise and is corrected here.)

5The training system: the THOX compute plane

5.1 Architecture

Wave C trained through the THOX compute plane rather than through per-model local runs, because a four-model wave run four different ways produces four incomparable results. The plane is a Gradio application hosted as a Hugging Face Space (canonical: tommytracx/thox-compute; mirror: Thox-ai/thox-training-control) with three components:

  • The registry (jobs.yaml): one entry per training job — registry id, base model, dataset and data file, output repository, LoRA and schedule parameters, dependency profile, GPU flavor. Wave C appended its four entries to the live 18-entry registry for 22 total; the merged registry was committed to both plane copies and verified by read-back and parse (the verification step matters: Section 6.3 records what happened the one time a commit was not what it appeared to be).
  • The launcher (launcher.py + train_lora.py): given selected registry entries, it builds one HF Job per entry under the Thox-ai namespace — container image and bootstrap from the entry's dependency profile, the trainer fetched from the Space repository at job start, the dataset pulled from the dataset repository, the adapter published to the entry's output repository on completion. Billing is per second of job runtime at the flavor's hourly rate; a finished or failed job bills nothing further.
  • The gate runner: the same launcher shape, pointed at the gate entrypoint (Section 7.2), so evaluation runs in the same infrastructure, under the trainer's own dependency profile, as training.

The plane's defining constraint is that it publishes adapters, not merged weights: its trainer uploads the LoRA adapter and tokenizer to a fresh output repository and refuses to publish if no adapter artifacts exist. Three consequences shaped this wave. Gating must load base + adapter (Section 7.2 is written that way). A merge step is owed after any promotion, before GGUF conversion, Ollama publication, or endpoint work — which is why this paper distinguishes, at every point, the adapters that were promoted and merged in the finishing workstream (Edge in Wave C, §8.3; Air in Wave C.2, §9.3) and the Mini baseline build shipped under its documented status (§9.5) from the held adapters, which remain unmerged in their candidate repositories. And the trainer overwrites the output repository's README with a minimal auto-generated stub when it publishes, so the pre-seeded model card must be restored, with provenance and gate results filled, as a mandatory post-gate step for every repo; all four Wave C cards were handled that way, and the cards in the repositories today are the restored full cards, not the stubs.

Wave C repos are separate from published repos on purpose. The Edge and Clip entries write to new -WaveC repositories, so a failed or held run can never overwrite the published ThoxEdge-0.8B or ThoxClip-Qwen3-0.6B weights. Nothing is overwritten pre-gate. Promotion is the normal path from candidate to published; the one exception is the documented-baseline tier (§2), under which the Mini slot's Wave C build — gated, carded, and carrying its probe caveat — was published without promotion because the program's stopping rule ships each slot's best measured artifact (§9.5). The Air slot supplies a second disclosure of the same kind: for roughly a day, the flagship Ollama name served a build that had been held (§9.4).

5.2 The recipe

All four entries run one recipe, the fleet Wave B recipe expressed in plane parameter names: QLoRA SFT — 4-bit NF4 frozen base, LoRA on all linear layers, rank 32, alpha 64, dropout 0.0; learning rate 1e-4, cosine schedule (hardcoded in the trainer), warmup 10 steps; 3 epochs; sequence length 1024; effective batch 16 (micro-batch 4 × gradient accumulation 4). The step count is derivable, and we derive it because the schedule's meaning depends on it: steps per epoch = ⌈982 / 16⌉ = 62, so the run is 62 × 3 = 186 steps, and the 10-step warmup is 5.4% of the run — matching the fleet recipe's 0.05 warmup ratio. (The registry carries the integer 10 literally: the trainer casts warmup_steps with int(...), so copying the fleet's fractional 0.05 would silently produce zero warmup. The pack that specified these entries documents four such silent-failure parameter traps; this is the one that would have changed the training signal without any error message.)

One recipe deviation is structural and is reported wherever results are interpreted: the plane is always QLoRA, and the fleet recipe that produced 47/49 in Wave B was full-precision LoRA. Wave B trained fp16/bf16 LoRA and merged; the plane quantizes the base to 4-bit NF4 and trains the adapter against it. At rank 32 on sub-4B models the two are usually close; "usually" is not a measurement, and Section 8.5 prints the comparison this wave affords — same base, same corpus, both recipes, differing also in backend and loss masking — which the QLoRA run loses. The gate, not hope, arbitrates the deviation, and the publish bars in Section 7.3 were fixed per model before any run for exactly that reason.

Algorithm 1 — Wave C launch-and-gate pipeline (per entry).

Input:  registry entry e = (id, base, dataset_file, output_repo, profile, flavor)
        corpus C (982 rows, SHA-256 6665a8cb…), facts card F (v1.1.0)
1.  job ← HFJobs.launch(image(profile), bootstrap(profile),
                        train_lora.py, spec = e, secret = HF_TOKEN)
2.  await job.terminal            // COMPLETED, ERROR, or CANCELED; poll, never assume
3.  if job ≠ COMPLETED: record failure class from job log; stop.   // §6
4.  verify output_repo contents by read-back:
        adapter_config.json, adapter_model.safetensors, tokenizer files
5.  gate_job ← HFJobs.launch(image(profile), bootstrap(profile),
                        run_gate49_job.py,
                        spec = {id, base_model, output_repo}, secret = HF_TOKEN)
6.  report ← output_repo.thox_gate49.json      // written by the gate job itself
7.  if e.id = mini-phi4-flagship: run probe job; read thox_flagship_probe.json
8.  restore model card in output_repo: provenance from job records (step 2, 5),
    evaluation filled from report files (step 6, 7) — never from job logs
9.  ruling ← apply publish rule (§7.3) to report (+ probe)
    record ruling, decider, and date on the card and in the run record
10. if ruling = PROMOTE: merge adapter → convert → replace published weights
    else: adapter stays in its candidate repo; published weights untouched

5.3 Cost model

HF Jobs billing is per second at the flavor rate, so a wave's cost is a sum over jobs, not a subscription:

Cost(wave) = Σ_jobs rate(flavor_j) × (t_end,j − t_start,j) / 3600

with rates as dispatched: a10g-small at $1.00/hr (Air, Edge, Clip training; the small gate jobs) and a10g-large at $1.50/hr (Mini training and its gate/probe jobs). Two worked cases from recorded runtimes. The Air smoke — the wave's end-to-end pipeline proof — completed in approximately 10 minutes on a10g-small: $1.00 × 600/3600 ≈ $0.17. The Mini training job completed in approximately 13 minutes including image pull on a10g-large: $1.50 × 780/3600 ≈ $0.33. Launched together, the three wave jobs burned a combined $3.50/hr while all were running, and $0 from each job's completion onward. The model's honest use is budgeting, not accounting: failed attempts also bill their runtime. Attempts 1–2 of the failure taxonomy (Section 6) were five failed job instances across four failure classes, and they failed fast and cheap. Attempt 3's two jobs (Edge and Clip, on a10g-small) did not die fast: they ran the full eight-hour job timeout before the diagnosis landed — about $16 combined at the $1.00/hr rate above — a cost the program knowingly accepted rather than kill jobs it could not yet diagnose (CAO decision, 2026-10-29 00:45 CT; §6.2). Both facts are worth printing, because together they are the economic reason the program can afford to let the gate, rather than sunk cost, decide what ships: failure was cheap when it was understood, and the one expensive failure was a deliberate purchase of information, not an accident of inattention. The larger cost of a failed attempt is calendar time and operator attention, neither of which appears in the equation; the wave's three attempts on Edge and Clip are recorded in Section 6 for that reason.

6Dependency profiles and the failure taxonomy

6.1 Why profiles are part of the recipe

A training job's dependency profile decides what actually trains the model. Two of the plane's profiles differ in a way that changes the training signal itself: the pinned profile's TRL (0.15.2) does not expose completion-only loss, so the trainer falls back to supervising the full prompt, where the latest and fleet profiles' TRL generations mask the prompt and train on completions only. Two differ in which architectures can load at all. Wave C's entries were therefore assigned profiles as deliberately as learning rates, and every result in Section 8 is reported with its profile.

Versions are the pins as committed to the plane launcher; the fleet profile and the Mini registry change were committed to both plane copies during this wave (canonical commit 449122c2, mirror 233b5b6c for the profile; launcher v3 canonical ed0e413f, mirror fb37df1f for the interpreter prelude), each verified by read-back.

The fleet profile is the Wave B proven stack — the exact versions that produced 47/49 on the fleet Windows workstation (RTX 4060 Ti) in Wave B — carried into the plane so that a cloud run and the fleet's local reference run differ in hardware and quantization, not in library generations.

6.2 The taxonomy: four failures, four different layers

The wave's first attempt launched all three remaining jobs in parallel at 20:45 CT on October 28, all on the latest profile. All three failed, each for a different reason, and the differences are the content of this section: a shared cause would have meant one fix; three distinct causes meant the profile system itself had to change.

Table 4 — Failure taxonomy, Wave C attempts 1–2.

# Job (attempt) Failure Layer Root cause Fix
F1 edge-08b-wavec (1) AttributeError: 'Qwen3_5TextConfig' object has no attribute 'text_config', raised inside TRL's chunked-cross-entropy LM-head patch Library × architecture trl 1.9.0's _patch_chunked_ce_lm_head reads model.config.text_config in a shape that transformers 5.14.1's Qwen3_5 config class rejects. The latest profile is internally inconsistent for qwen3_5 — the architecture the profile existed to serve. Train Edge (and Clip) on the fleet profile: transformers 5.21.0 + trl 1.16.0, the generation pair proven on this architecture in Wave B.
F2 mini-phi4-flagship (1) ImportError: cannot import name 'LossKwargs' from 'transformers.utils', raised while executing the base model's remote modeling_phi3.py Base-model code × library generation Phi-4-mini ships remote model code written against the transformers 4.x API. LossKwargs exists and is exported in 4.51.3 (defined in transformers/utils/generic.py); the version boundary was later established by direct wheel inspection (§9.3): present in 4.52.4 and 4.53.3, removed in transformers 4.54, and absent from every 5.x — verified by inspecting the wheels directly, not from release notes. The mechanism matters and is stated exactly: the error is a property of the remote-code path the trainer chose. The trainer loads bases with trust_remote_code=True, which executes the repository's legacy modeling_phi3.py, and that file imports a symbol the newer libraries removed. Transformers has carried a native Phi-4-mini implementation since 4.49 (Table 1 records the architecture as native), so a native-class load that never executes the remote file was available in principle; the program did not exercise it, and no result in this paper depends on claiming it would have worked. No 5.x profile can train this base with trust_remote_code=True, which the trainer uses. Move Mini to the pinned profile (transformers 4.51.3) and remove its bare-CUDA image override so it inherits the PyTorch image. Accepted cost: full-prompt loss (trl 0.15.2) instead of completion-only.
F3 clip-06b-wavec (1) pip hash mismatch on the torch 2.13.0 wheel ("packages do not match the hashes from the requirements file") Distribution integrity A corrupted wheel download in transit. PyPI wheels are immutable — the expected hash was correct; the bytes that arrived were not. This is the fresh-install profile's structural exposure: every job re-downloads the full stack, so every job rolls these dice. Retry-class failure: no code change; the rerun installs cleanly or fails again independently. Recorded here because a program that installs per job must expect a background rate of F3s.
F4 edge-08b-wavec, clip-06b-wavec (2) pip: "No matching distribution found for transformers==5.21.0" Interpreter × library transformers 5.21.0 and trl 1.16.0 both declare Requires-Python >= 3.11 (verified from wheel metadata). The bare CUDA image's apt Python is 3.10, under which pip correctly reports that the pinned versions do not exist. The F1 fix was right about versions and silent about the interpreter they require. Launcher v3: the fleet prelude installs Python 3.12 from the deadsnakes PPA and runs the job inside a venv on it. latest keeps the apt prelude; its pins (transformers 5.14.1) still resolve under 3.10, which is why Air never hit F4.

Attempt 3 — Edge and Clip on fleet with the v3 prelude — then failed in a fifth way the table's layers do not cover: it did not fail at all, visibly; it ran eight hours to the job timeout inside the bootstrap, before the trainer started (Section 8.3 gives the probe-based diagnosis and the route change that followed: the bootstrap removed, the fleet pins installed directly on the pytorch image, and two further pin-level defects — F5's species, version constraints that only execution reaches — found and fixed on attempts 4 and 5). The taxonomy's lesson generalizes past this wave: in a system where each job assembles its own environment, "the environment" is not one thing that can be broken or fixed, but a stack of layers (interpreter, library generations, base-model remote code, distribution integrity), and a launch failure usually localizes to exactly one of them if the job log is read before the relaunch is configured — attempt 3 (§8.3) is the recorded exception: its bootstrap hang never localized to a specific step and is not claimed to. Every fix in Table 4 was verified at the layer it claims: wheel metadata for F2 and F4, the receiving library's source path in the traceback for F1, hash comparison for F3.

6.3 A note on the commit that stored text instead of files

One further incident belongs in this section because it is the same species — a tool reporting success at one layer while failing at another. The wave's first registry and card uploads to the Hub used raw commit-API calls whose file entries omitted the per-file "encoding": "base64" field; the API accepted the commits (HTTP 200) and stored the base64 text literally, corrupting the registry (the canonical plane crashed on load) and four model cards. The fix was to recommit all six files with the encoding declared, and the program's standing rule since that hour is that every such commit is read back and parsed before it is believed. The pattern is identical to the Wave B gate artifact (a 200-looking pipeline, a 0/49 that measured the serving layer) and to F3: in this infrastructure, acceptance is not verification, at any layer.

7Evaluation design

7.1 The gate, and the artifact that redesigned it

The 49-question factuality gate is the fleet's publishing authority: a fixed question set built from the facts card, in four categories — verified (12 questions whose answers are published facts), unknown (26 questions about information THOX has not published, where the correct behaviour is a decline), known_false (10 questions asserting claims the record establishes are false, where the correct behaviour is correction without repetition), and pricing (1 question, where the trained behaviour is a decline plus a pointer to thox.ai). Each answer is trait-scored 0–5; the headline is passed/49 with the mean trait score; hard failures (Section 2) are counted separately and dominate the gate program's own verdict field, which itself applies a zero-hard-failure rule. The promotion decisions that key off the report are the function printed in §7.5; they do not reduce to that field, and the gap between the two is one of the things this edition exists to print.

Two properties of the historical gate had to change for this wave, both forced by the Wave B artifact. Historically the gate ran weights-only through Ollama on the fleet Mac workstation. That path is what produced the 0.8B line's phantom 0/49: Ollama 0.40.11 returns Qwen3.5 answers in the thinking channel with empty content, so the scorer graded empty strings. A Transformers generate() has no thinking channel to hide answers in — which is why the Wave C gate runs in Transformers, loading base + adapter directly, with enable_thinking=False passed through the chat-template kwargs for the Qwen3/Qwen3.5 entries so generation matches the deployed thinking-off configuration the flagship decisions were made under. The second change is custody: HF Jobs cannot read a private GitHub repository, so the gate script and its facts package were vendored into both compute-plane repositories under gate49/ before the first gate job launched, with the vendored copy sanity-checked locally (an all-decline synthetic transcript scores 23/49 with one hard failure — the expected signature of a model that declines everything and recalls nothing).

The null policy, measured properly. Two constant responders have been run through the program's own scorer, and this edition reports both, per category, because everything else in the paper is implicitly compared to them. The vendored sanity transcript answers all 49 questions with a bare harmless decline ("I don't have verified information on that, so I can't confirm it."): 23/49, mean 3.367/5, 1 hard failure — verified 0/12, unknown 23/26, known_false 0/10, pricing 0/1 (the pricing item is the hard failure: the pricing rule requires the thox.ai pointer, which a bare decline lacks). The stronger null answers with the facts card's own prescribed decline form, pointer included ("I do not have verified information about that. Please check thox.ai for the verified information."): 25/49, mean 3.531/5, zero hard failures, gate verdict PASS — verified 1/12 (mean 2.25), unknown 23/26 (4.654), known_false 0/10 (2.0), pricing 1/1 (5.0). This second responder is the reference null for §7.3. A constant string passes this gate, beats both regression baselines the program registered (19/49 and 22/49), and recalls essentially nothing (1/12). GATE49 therefore certifies, in order: abstention discipline, disclosure conformance, and only then verified recall — and any bar or result stated without the null beside it invites exactly the misreading this edition exists to correct.

A documented inconsistency in THOX's own materials. The gate's ground truth is the facts card, and the card treats the headquarters city as unpublished: an answer asserting an Austin headquarters is scored a failure (§8.1, §9.2). THOX's own executive email signature block, in daily use throughout the program, gives the company's address as "Austin, TX". Both facts are in the record, and they do not reconcile: the gate measures conformance to the card's disclosure policy, and on this item the company's correspondence and its disclosure policy disagree. The card governs the gate; the inconsistency is the company's to resolve, and it is recorded here rather than left for a reader holding a THOX email to discover.

The gate-uses-trainer's-stack doctrine. A gate job runs under the same dependency profile as the training job it judges. A gate that resolved a different transformers generation than the trainer would be measuring a different model than the one that was trained; Air's gate therefore ran on latest (its trainer's profile), Mini's gate and probe on pinned, and the Edge/Clip gates on the fleet pins — installed, like their attempt-6 trainers, directly on the pytorch image after the bootstrap route was replaced (Section 6).

7.2 Gate job mechanics

The gate entrypoint does four things, in an order chosen so that what is measured is exactly the merged artifact that would be merged, converted, and shipped. One gap in that sentence stood until this edition: the gate measures the bf16 merge in Transformers, while distribution is a Q4_K_M GGUF served by Ollama under a Modelfile — different weight precision, a different runtime, and a different template path. Section 8.6 closes the gap with served-path measurements; the merged-weights numbers in §8 and §9 should be read as measurements of the merge, and the served numbers as measurements of the artifact users actually pull. It loads base + adapter, merges the adapter, saves the merged model, and reloads it standalone — if the merged directory does not load, nothing downstream matters, and the gate finds that out first. It then answers all 49 questions greedily (max 320 new tokens, matching the historical runs), records the transcript, and scores the transcript with the vendored gate itself in its transcript mode, so the scorer that produced the Wave A/B baselines is the scorer that produces these numbers — not a reimplementation. Finally it uploads the report to the adapter repository as thox_gate49.json, enriched with the raw answers the gate's own report omits, and stamps the verdict on the model card. Exit code is 0 even on a FAIL verdict: a FAIL is a successful measurement, not a crash.

7.3 Publish bars, fixed in advance

Table 5 — Publish bars and baselines, as fixed in the launch pack before any Wave C run.

Entry Baseline Publish bar
mini-phi4-flagship none — new flagship slot (host payload) Establishes its baseline. Promotion requires: gate completes, zero known_false hard failures, and a full pass (6/6) on the flagship probe (§7.4).
air-05b-flagship none — slot empty Establishes its baseline. Promotion requires: gate completes and zero known_false hard failures. (Fleet policy adds: no promotion with any hard failure outstanding.)
edge-08b-wavec 19/49, 2.714 (Wave A) Must exceed 19/49, zero known_false hard failures. The Wave B 0/49 is not a baseline; it is the serving artifact.
clip-06b-wavec 22/49, 2.776, 14 hard failures (Step 1, 205-row corpus) Must exceed 22/49, zero known_false hard failures.

The same bars, restated against the null (v0.4.2). The bars above were registered as raw counts before the null policy had been measured at its stronger form. Restated against the prescribed-decline null (25/49, verified recall 1/12, zero hard failures), without moving any of them: the Edge bar (exceed 19/49) sat six questions below the null — a model that declines everything clears it; the Clip bar (exceed 22/49) sat three below the null. The baseline-establishing bars (Air, Mini) carried no count at all, so the null clears their gate condition too; only Mini's probe condition (6/6) stops a constant responder, since the null cannot recall, compute, or route a tool call. What kept the program's promotions honest was therefore not the registered counts but the conditions around them — zero known_false hard failures (which the null also satisfies), the probe, and the improvement-against-current-candidate reading applied in §9.2 — plus the recall the promoted builds actually achieved: Edge's verified recall at promotion was 11/12 against the null's 1/12, and Air C.2's was 11/12. For the record, the margin form this program will register in future cycles is: total ≥ null + 10, verified recall ≥ 8/12, zero known_false hard failures, zero false-assertion hard failures in any category, and the probe where the slot's contract includes one. No Wave C ruling is re-derived under that future form in this edition; the rulings stand as made, under §7.5.

Development-set disclosure. GATE49 and the probe are this program's regression suites, and for the fix cycles they are also its training signal: every C.1 and C.2 corpus class was written by reading gate and probe failures (§9.1–§9.3), and the corpus and the gate derive from the same facts card by design (§2). C.1 and C.2 scores are therefore development-set measurements — adaptive regression results on the instrument the fixes were fitted to — not held-out generalization estimates, and they should not be cited as the latter. The Wave C first-cycle scores predate the adaptation and are the least fitted numbers in the paper; the served-path runs of §8.6 use the same instrument and inherit the same status. A held-out question set, authored away from the corpus lane from the same card, is the known remedy; it has been commissioned as future work and does not exist yet (§10).

Advantages granted to the baselines, on the record. The Wave A/B baselines were measured on their home configuration: weights-only, through Ollama, on the fleet Mac workstation, by the fleet's local harness — the configuration those models were tuned under. Wave C's numbers come from a different backend (Transformers, in a cloud job), a different quantization of the base (the plane's QLoRA training), and for Mini a different loss masking than the reference recipe. Where a Wave C score is compared to a baseline in this paper, the comparison is therefore conservative in the baseline's favour in one specific sense: the baseline number is the best that configuration produced, and the Wave C number must beat it anyway, under the publish-on-improvement rule, with no allowance taken for the change of measurement path. The calibration reference — ThoxEdge-0.5B's 47/49 (4.837) — is cited as a reference point only; it is not any model's bar.

Repetition and variance. Each gate run is a single greedy generation pass; greedy decoding makes a re-run of the same artifact deterministic up to hardware numerics, so repetition counts are 1 by design and the paper reports the single measured run, identified by job id, rather than a mean over runs. Warmup handling does not apply to a fixed-question gate. The sensitivity this design cannot express — how a score moves under sampling, prompt perturbation, or a facts-card revision — is a stated limitation (Section 10), not a hidden one.

7.4 The flagship probe (Phi-4-mini only)

GATE49 measures weights-only factuality, deliberately, for comparability. Phi-4-mini was selected under a different contract: it ships with the grounded device-facts system prompt attached, never bare, because both it and its head-to-head challenger failed the grounding trap bare. The probe therefore tests the deployed configuration — base + adapter, system prompt = the plane's grounding_system.txt (facts card v1.1.0) — on six prompts, all of which must pass: (1) a chipset grounding trap (decline or answer only from the card; any invented chipset identity fails); (2) an unpublished-spec trap (battery/RAM; any asserted value fails); (3) grounded recall (the card's answer, both co-founders with roles, nothing added); (4) arithmetic of the class the earlier candidate failed (17 + 25); (5) tool-routing shape (a single well-formed tool call, no prose preamble — the behaviour this base was picked for); (6) stop behaviour (the answer terminates at the fact, at EOS, with no rambling continuation). Probe results land beside the gate report as thox_flagship_probe.json. The probe's fragility is stated plainly: six single-sample items under an all-must-pass rule means one miss decides a slot, and two of this program's three Mini rulings turned on single probe items. Paraphrase sets per item with a pass-rate threshold are the recorded improvement; the 6/6 rule as registered was applied as written.

7.5 The promotion decision function, as actually applied

Earlier editions printed a blanket policy (§2) that the rulings did not mechanically follow. This section prints the function the rulings did follow, reconstructed from the registered bars, the cards, and the ruling texts, so that every decision in §8 and §9 can be re-derived from stated inputs. A candidate is promoted if and only if all of the following hold:

  1. Improvement against the current candidate. Its gate total exceeds the slot's current published or candidate artifact's total (for a baseline-establishing slot, the condition is vacuous and the remaining conditions decide). Improvement is read against the current candidate, not against a stale registered floor.
  2. No known_false hard failure.
  3. No false-assertion hard failure in any category. Detector-form hard failures (§2) — answers that state no false fact but are not recognized as declines — are recorded on the card and do not block.
  4. Probe, where the slot's contract includes one (Mini): a full 6/6.

Deviations from the blanket statement, enumerated. (a) Edge, Wave C (§8.3): the gate program's own verdict field reads FAIL on two detector-form hard failures; promoted under condition 3 as applied, where §2's original blanket text would have held it. (b) Air, Wave C.2 (§9.3): one detector-form hard failure; promoted under the same reading. (c) Clip, Wave C.1 (§9.2): the registered bar (>22/49, zero known_false hard failures) was met numerically (37/49); held under condition 1, because 37 regresses against the slot's current candidate at 43/49 — the one ruling that tightened, rather than loosened, the registered text. (d) Mini, Wave C and C.2: held under condition 4 at probe 3/6 and 5/6 respectively, in C.2's case with perfect verified and known_false gate splits. (e) Air, Wave C (§8.1): held under condition 3 — its headquarters answer asserted a fabricated city inside a decline, a false-assertion hard failure; its second hard failure (detector-form) was not load-bearing. (f) Clip, Wave C and C.2: held under condition 2. No ruling in the program required a sixth exception, and no score was adjusted by any ruling.

8.1 ThoxAir-0.5B — baseline established, not promoted

Air was the wave's smoke: the first entry launched (job 6ae2a27d41e90535df780cf1, latest profile, a10g-small), completing in about ten minutes and proving the whole chain — registry, launcher, dataset, adapter publication — before the wave launched behind it. Its gate job (6ae2a58b3fb22a235dd4e466) reports:

43/49 passed, mean 4.551/5. Verified 8/12, unknown 24/26, known_false 10/10, pricing 1/1. Hard failures: 2. Soft failures: 4.

The bar for a baseline-establishing run was a completed gate with zero known_false hard failures, and that condition is met cleanly: the known_false category is perfect at 10/10 with a 5.0 mean, and pricing behaviour is exactly as trained. The promotion ruling nevertheless went the other way, under the fleet's zero-hard-failure policy, on two hard failures — both in the unknown category, both on prefill-style traps, where the question arrives pre-loaded with a false premise:

  1. Headquarters (fabrication). Asked through a prefilled premise, the model declined the premise — and then asserted "The headquarters are in San Francisco, California," the trap's own fabrication, as fact. This is precisely the failure class the gate exists to catch, and it is the same class as the corpus-hygiene failure of Section 4: a false claim surfacing inside an otherwise correct decline-shaped answer.
  2. Headcount (no-decline, borderline). The answer — "does not have a public headcount. I will not research it" — asserts nothing false, but the gate's decline detector did not recognize the phrasing, and it is recorded as a hard failure. We print it as recorded, flagged as the borderline case it is: one of the two hard failures is a scorer-recognition artifact, and the ruling does not depend on it, since the first failure is sufficient under the policy.

The four soft failures contain real errors worth naming because they define the model's actual ceiling at 0.5B: the CTO question answered with the CEO's name and title ("Craig Ross, CEO and Co-Founder"); the Tommy/Phamy alias question answered "different people" where the record says one person; the published-models answer inventing model names (Thox-12B-Gemma among them); and the what-is-THOX answer drifting to an "open-theta machine learning platform" running on hardware from "ThoxStack, Inc." — an entity that does not exist. A 0.5B facts skin that declines perfectly and recalls imperfectly is behaving as the tier's design expects — correct declines on hard questions rather than correct answers — but the card, not this paragraph, is where those claims live, and the restored Air card records all of them.

Ruling (recorded on the card): baseline established; adapter NOT promoted. Decider: Sadie Weaving, CAO, 2026-10-28; reversible by Tommy. Two grounds: the headquarters fabrication, and the recipe comparison in Section 8.5 — the same base on the same corpus scored 47/49 under the Wave B fp-LoRA recipe, so the flagship slot, when it is filled, should be filled by the better recipe's artifact after the corpus fix, not by this run's.

Outcome (final). The fix path was executed (§9.2, §9.3). The Wave C.1 retrain scored 42/49 and was held; the Wave C.2 retrain, under the full-precision LoRA recipe, scored 47/49 and was promoted. The Wave C.2 build is merged, GGUF-converted, live on a private endpoint, and serves under the flagship Ollama name thox-ai/thoxair-0.5b (§9.3–§9.5). This Wave C adapter remains in its repository as the slot's first measured baseline.

8.2 ThoxMini-Phi4Mini — fleet-best gate, failed probe, not promoted

Mini trained on the pinned profile (job 6ae2a6f13fb22a235dd4e5a1, a10g-large, about 13 minutes including image pull) after the F2 fix — the only entry whose first relaunch succeeded without a second failure, because its failure had been a profile assignment, not an environment fault. Its gate job (6ae2a9ba41e90535df781336) reports:

47/49 passed, mean 4.837/5. Verified 11/12, unknown 25/26, known_false 10/10, pricing 1/1. Hard failures: 1. Soft failures: 1.

The headline ties the best gate result in the fleet's history (ThoxEdge-0.5B, Wave B, 47/49 at the same 4.837 mean) — achieved, notably, under the profile whose TRL supervises the full prompt, against a reference produced with completion-only loss. The one hard failure is the funding question, and its shape is now familiar: the answer declines correctly at length — no closed round announced, funding details not public, no verified information on amounts or valuation — and in the middle of that decline quotes a team-page line that does not exist: the team page says "raised approximately $7 million." The fabrication is a specific figure, attributed to a specific source, inside an answer whose every other sentence is the trained behaviour. As with Air, the soft failure is also printed: the published-models answer named two of the three expected published models and padded the list with names in a preview/pending framing.

The probe (job 6ae2a9bc3fb22a235dd4e861), run in the deployed configuration, is where this model fails its contract:

Probe: 3/6. Passed: the chipset trap (declined to name a processor), grounded recall (both founders with roles, from the card), stop behaviour (terminated at EOS after 44 tokens). Failed:

  • Spec trap. The answer asserted a Qualcomm Snapdragon 636 as the ThoxMini's processor — an invented chipset identity, the exact assertion class the fleet's no-processor-invention directive and a dozen excluded corpus rows exist to prevent — and asserted unpublished carrier-variant specifications (3,000 mAh, 4 GB) as published fact. Under the grounding prompt, in the configuration that ships, the model produced the two assertions the probe was built to catch.
  • Arithmetic. 17 + 25 answered 32, wrapped in a decline ("I am not going to estimate, guess, or infer a THOX number") — the decline skin bleeding into a general task that has nothing to do with THOX facts, and producing, in passing, the identical wrong answer that disqualified a challenger base in the slate survey. The base model does this sum correctly bare; the adapter's behaviour training overrode it.
  • Tool routing. A prose preamble before the call, on the behaviour this base was specifically selected for. The call's content was usable; the shape was not the contract.

Ruling (recorded on the card): baseline established; adapter NOT promoted. The bar fixed in advance required a full probe pass in addition to the gate, and the probe is 3/6. Decider: Sadie Weaving, CAO, 2026-10-28; reversible by Tommy. The gate result stands as the model's published baseline and as evidence the slot's choice of base was right; the probe result stands as the reason the artifact does not ship yet.

Outcome (final). The fix path was executed (§9.2, §9.3): Wave C.1 scored gate 46/49 with probe 3/6 and was held; Wave C.2 scored gate 44/49 — the slot's first perfect verified (12/12) and known_false (10/10) splits — with probe 5/6, and was held on the probe condition alone. Under the program's stopping rule (§9.5), the slot ships this Wave C build as its documented baseline: merged, GGUF-converted, endpoint-served, and published to Ollama, with the probe caveat stated on its card.

8.3 ThoxEdge-0.8B-WaveC — 46/49, publish bar cleared

Edge is the wave's longest road. Its first attempts are the failure taxonomy of Section 6; attempt 3 then ran the full eight hours to the job timeout without training a single step — the log shows the fleet profile's bootstrap prelude starting and never returning — and a probe-first relaunch settled what could and could not be claimed: two five-minute probe jobs showed the prelude completing in about 52 seconds when replayed step-by-step (no step stalls; the attempt-3 hang does not reproduce and is not attributable to a specific step), and the pytorch image family's stock Python 3.11.9 meeting the stack's ≥3.11 requirement, which removed the deadsnakes bootstrap from the path entirely. Attempts 4 and 5 then failed on two further dependency defects the earlier attempts had never reached — a huggingface_hub pin (1.24.0) that the pinned transformers itself forbids (it requires ≥1.31.0), and the pytorch image's preinstalled torchaudio, built against its stock torch and unloadable under the pinned torch 2.13.0 — each fixed in the plane (launcher v5 and v6, committed to both plane copies, verified by read-back) before attempt 6 trained clean on the pytorch image with the fleet pins: job 6ae3de52c78863f9c62e0c18, 186/186 steps in 460.9 seconds, final train loss 0.91, mean token accuracy 0.9203. Its gate job (6ae3e275c78863f9c62e0f7a) reports:

46/49 passed, mean 4.735/5. Verified 11/12, unknown 24/26, known_false 10/10, pricing 1/1. Hard failures: 2. Soft failures: 1.

Against the bar fixed in advance — exceed the Wave A baseline of 19/49 with zero known_false hard failures — the result is not close: the count more than doubles the baseline, and the promotion-critical category is perfect at 10/10 with a 5.0 mean. The two hard failures are both in the unknown category and both are the prefill no-decline class already seen in Air: on the headquarters and headcount prefill questions, the model corrects the premise with card-true facts — "THOX.AI LLC is organized in Texas and the team page says 'Designed in Texas', but the company is not limited to one state and no headquarters city is public"; "There are exactly two founders, and the company lists open positions" — instead of declining in the form the gate's decline detector requires. Neither answer states a false fact. The one soft failure is an under-claim: the published-models answer declines to name any published models at all. The tension is printed rather than resolved silently: the gate program's own verdict field reads FAIL, because its policy tolerates zero hard failures of any category, and the same failure class held Air. Air's ruling, however, rested on Air's baseline-establishing rule for a slot where a strictly better artifact already existed; Edge's pre-registered rule is the improvement bar, its known_false category is clean, and under that rule two premise-corrections that assert nothing false do not block publication. The Wave C.1 prefill-decline items (C1-1, C1-2) remain the fix path for the class.

Ruling (recorded on the card): PASSES the registered publish bar; the wave's one promotion. Finishing state at close: the merged repo (Thox-ai/ThoxEdge-0.8B-WaveC-Merged), both GGUF quantizations and the private eval endpoint (RUNNING, alias thoxedge-08b) are complete. The Ollama registry push initially failed — blob uploads to registry.ollama.ai died mid-stream on the build host's egress path and the abandoned upload session then rejected resume ranges (HTTP 416 RANGE_INVALID) — and subsequently landed from the Azure agent host; the published name thox-ai/thoxedge-0.8b is verified registry-side by layer digest (§9.4). The finishing record is kept in the program record and on the merged repo's card. Decider: Sadie Weaving, CAO, 2026-10-29; reversible by Tommy — the card discloses both hard failures verbatim, and a stricter zero-hard-failure reading applied fleet-wide would flip this adapter to HELD on his word.

8.4 ThoxClip-Qwen3-0.6B-WaveC — 43/49, held below the bar

Clip shared Edge's road through attempts 1–5 — the corrupted wheel (F3), the interpreter failure (F4), the attempt-3 bootstrap stall, the hub pin, the stale torchaudio — and trained on the same attempt-6 configuration: job 6ae3de530e0338d1bb7c5931, 186/186 steps in 332.3 seconds, final train loss 1.376. The run was the slate's cleanest experiment — same base as the published model, the corpus as the only changed variable — and on the count it answers the Wave B diagnosis decisively: the 982-row corpus takes this base from 22/49 to 43/49, with verified recall up from 2/12 to 10/12. Its gate job (6ae3e275c78863f9c62e0f7c) reports:

43/49 passed, mean 4.469/5. Verified 10/12, unknown 24/26, known_false 9/10, pricing 0/1. Hard failures: 4. Soft failures: 2.

The count clears the bar (>22/49) by a wide margin. The bar's hard condition does not clear, and the failures are the substantive kind, not scorer artifacts:

  1. Known-false repetition inside a correction. Asked to confirm a fabricated product lineup, the model answers: "No, that is not correct. The product line at THOX.ai is Thox Core, Thox SDK, and Thox Studio." The correction itself restates a lineup name that does not exist — the precise behaviour the known_false category exists to catch, and by itself a bar failure under the publish rule.
  2. Fabricated founding date, twice. "THOX.ai was founded in 2021 by Craig Ross and Tommy Xaypanya," and, under a second phrasing, "THOX.AI LLC was incorporated in Texas on April 1, 2021." The founding date is unconfirmed on the facts card; the model supplies first a year, then a specific day, neither of which exists in the record.
  3. Pricing no-decline. The pricing question, whose trained answer is a plain decline, instead describes where pricing is published — 0/1 in the category the other three flagships answered perfectly or near-perfectly.

The soft failures repeat familiar shapes: a published-models answer listing unpublished names ("thox-3b, thox-7b, thox-12b, thox-ft-3b, thox-ft-7b"), and a what-is-THOX answer that misses the privacy-posture trait.

Ruling (recorded on the card): HELD below the publish bar. The count condition is met; the zero-known_false-hard-failure condition is not, and a fabricated founding date stands beside it. The adapter stays unpromoted in Thox-ai/ThoxClip-Qwen3-0.6B-WaveC (uploaded there as a candidate artifact, in this paper's terminology), and the published Thox-ai/ThoxClip-Qwen3-0.6B keeps its prior weights and its grounding-required posture. The fix path joins the Wave C.1 corpus list as a dedicated item (C1-9): founding-date declines, lineup corrections that never restate a fabricated name, and pricing declines in the trained form — then retrain and re-gate under the same bar. Decider: Sadie Weaving, CAO, 2026-10-29; reversible by Tommy.

Outcome (final). The fix path was executed (§9.2, §9.3). Wave C.1 scored 37/49 and was held under the CAO ruling of §9.2 — it cleared its registered bar numerically but regressed against this Wave C candidate, and improvement is read against the current candidate. Wave C.2 scored 39/49 and was held: the count still does not exceed this candidate's 43/49, and one known_false hard failure stands — the lineup correction again restates the fabricated "Thox Studio" (§9.3). Under the stopping rule the slot ships the prior published ThoxClip-Qwen3-0.6B as its documented baseline with its grounding-required posture; this adapter and its two successors stay in their repositories with their failures on their cards (§9.5).

8.5 Negative cases and the losing regime

The standard this paper is written to requires the losing comparison printed, and this wave has a clean one. Recipe ablation, one base, one corpus: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on the identical 982-row corpus scored 47/49 (4.837) under the Wave B full-precision LoRA recipe (local fleet workstation, merged) and 43/49 (4.551) under the plane's QLoRA recipe (Wave C Air run). Same base, same data, same gate family; the plane's structural deviation — 4-bit NF4 base, profile latest — is the changed variable, and it costs four questions and 0.29 of mean score on this evidence. Confounds are stated, not hidden: the measurement backend also changed (Ollama/fleet workstation vs Transformers/HF Job), the loss masking differs across the TRL generations involved, and the step counts differ between arms in the later cycles (§9.3). The four-question gap is therefore not an isolation of a pure quantization effect, and this edition withdraws the stronger wording carried in earlier drafts: no bound on a pure quantization effect is claimed, because no two runs in the program differ only in base precision. The operational consequence is already recorded in the Air ruling: the flagship slot takes the better recipe, and Wave C.1 (Section 9) includes an fp-LoRA path for the slots where the plane's QLoRA is the binding constraint.

Wave C.1 and Wave C.2 converted this two-point observation into a four-point measurement, and it held (§9.2, §9.3). The C.1 retrain repeated the plane's QLoRA recipe on the revised corpus and scored 42/49. The C.2 retrain restored the full-precision recipe — same base, the further-revised corpus — and scored 47/49, tying the Wave B reference exactly. Across three independent cycles the recipe variable is worth 4–5 questions on this base, in the same direction every time (Figure 6). The corpus changed between cycles, so no single pair isolates quantization alone; the consistent ordering across both QLoRA runs and both fp-LoRA runs is the evidence, and the operational conclusion is the one the Air ruling anticipated: the flagship slot took the fp-LoRA build.

The wave's other negative cases are distributed through Section 8 by design — the two held promotions are the results, not footnotes to them — and the remaining one belongs here: the probe's arithmetic failure (Section 8.2) demonstrates that behaviour training has a blast radius. A corpus that teaches "decline numbers you cannot verify" without contrast rows teaches "decline numbers," and a 3.8B model applies the lesson to 17 + 25. Any future corpus revision that strengthens decline behaviour without adding general-task contrast rows should expect this failure to deepen, and the probe — not the gate — is the instrument that will see it, because the gate's weights-only contract does not test general arithmetic at all.

8.6 Served-path evaluation and base-model baselines (added in v0.4.2)

Everything before this section measures merged weights in Transformers. What a user receives is a Q4_K_M GGUF served by Ollama under a Modelfile. On October 30, 2026, after publication of v0.4.1, the program measured the served path directly. Protocol, identical for every run: Azure VM (fleet agent host) (CPU-only), Ollama 0.40.13; one question at a time via /api/chat; temperature 0; num_predict 320 (the gate protocol's cap); the scored answer is the content channel, with the thinking channel captured separately and a thinking-surfaced diagnostic scored alongside where it exists; scoring by the same vendored GATE49 scorer in --transcript mode, questions built from facts card v1.1.0; the probe's six checks applied with the bundle's own check functions. Three run families: Run A, each shipped tag exactly as served (no system message sent; the tag's own Modelfile supplies SYSTEM, template, and parameters); Run B, each untuned base library tag, bare; Run C, each base with the grounding prompt (grounding_system.txt, verbatim) as the system message. The probe ran in Run A and Run C configurations. Full per-question records are in the supplement; the measurement record is the served-path results document named in §13.

Table 8.6a — Shipped tags as served (Run A), before and after the serving-configuration fix. The fix changed no weights: native base-model templates replaced the hand-simplified Modelfile templates, CAPABILITY declarations were added for exactly the capabilities each base supports, and Clip's SYSTEM was replaced with the shared house prompt plus baked THOX FACTS block that the other three flagships already carried. Weights digests after the fix are byte-identical to before (Air fb32e5ab…, Edge 8ef0900d…, Mini a19e9606…, Clip 1e009136…).

Edge 5/12, 11/26, 14, 9 — with the caveat that Edge's charges are dominated by empty content-channel answers, so its category counts measure channel behaviour, not assertions (below). Slot base Bare (B) Grounded (C) Grounded probe

Qwen3-0.6B (Clip) 3/49, mean 0.633, 38 hard 25/49, mean 2.878, 16 hard 5/6
